name: Jainism (Jaina dharma)
alt_names: Nirgrantha / Niggaṇṭha dharma (the 'knotless' ones; the name in Pali and early Prakrit sources)
regions: Magadha and Videha (Bihar) — the homeland of Mahāvīra

tradition.text: beginningless: the dharma is re-proclaimed by twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in every half of each time-cycle; in this descending half the first was Ṛṣabha and the last Mahāvīra (nirvāṇa traditionally 527 BCE)

scholarly.text: Pārśva (probably historical) c. 8th–7th c. BCE; Mahāvīra 6th–5th c. BCE (nirvāṇa dated by scholars between c. 527 and c. 425 BCE)

transmissions_received.what: the wider śramaṇa milieu of wandering renunciation, karma, rebirth and release shared with the Ājīvikas and Buddhists
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly account; the tradition itself regards its dharma as beginningless and not derived from any other

transmissions_given.what: Kundakunda's niścaya teaching, read by Banārsīdās and the Adhyātma circle
Tamil didactic verse forms and ethics (contested; see dsp:affiliation-of-tirukkural)

distinctive_positions: Innumerable individual souls (jīva), each by nature endowed with infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy, obscured by karma conceived as subtle matter that binds to the soul
No creator or controlling God; the universe (loka) is uncreated and eternal, running through endless ascending and descending time-cycles
Non-harm (ahiṃsā) toward all six classes of living beings, including earth-, water-, fire-, wind- and plant-bodied beings, as the pure and eternal law proclaimed by all Arhats
Liberation by right faith, right knowledge and right conduct (with austerity), by one's own effort; the liberated soul (siddha) rises to the summit of the universe and remains individual
Twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras ('ford-makers') in each half-cycle, who found the fourfold community (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen)
Many-sidedness (anekānta), standpoints (naya) and conditional predication (syādvāda) as the way of stating truth
Voluntary, peaceful death by gradual fasting (sallekhanā) as the culmination of a disciplined life — under strict conditions (restricted; summary only)
summary: The Jain tradition of the Jinas ('conquerors'), re-proclaimed in this era by Ṛṣabha and, last, by Vardhamāna Mahāvīra, a contemporary of the Buddha. It teaches the eternal reality of innumerable souls and of matter, karma as subtle matter binding the soul through passion and activity, and liberation through the three jewels, austerity and non-harm. It divided into the Śvetāmbara ('white-clad') and Digambara ('sky-clad') traditions, with the Yāpanīya between them, and within the Śvetāmbaras into image-worshipping and non-image-worshipping orders.

name: Śvetāmbara

tradition.text: the continuous line of Sudharman; the canon redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa)

scholarly.text: a distinct Śvetāmbara identity is visible from roughly the early centuries CE (Mathurā inscriptions name gaṇas and kulas matching the Kalpa Sūtra's list); the canon was fixed in writing in the 5th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Monks and nuns wear white garments and carry bowls; holding clothes and bowls without attachment is not 'possession' (parigraha is defined as attachment, mūrcchā)
The naked, solitary Jinakalpa mode was followed by the Jinas and early monks but lapsed after Jambū; the Sthavirakalpa (living in groups with minimal equipment) is the valid mode now
Women can attain liberation in a female body; the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara Mallī was a woman
The omniscient (kevalin) continues to take food while his body lasts
The canon of Āgamas survives in large part (the twelfth Aṅga, the Dṛṣṭivāda with the fourteen Pūrvas, is lost)
In Mahāvīra's life: the transfer of the embryo from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to the kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā; fourteen dreams of the mother; Mahāvīra's marriage to Yaśodā
summary: The 'white-clad' branch of the Jain tradition, which preserves the Ardhamāgadhī canon of Āgamas redacted at Valabhī and holds that women can reach liberation and that the omniscient eats. It comprises the image-worshipping Mūrtipūjakas (organized in gacchas) and the two non-image-worshipping orders, the Sthānakavāsīs and the Terāpanthīs.

name: Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka
alt_names: Caityavāsī (historically, a different sense: temple-dwelling monks)
distinctive_positions: Accepts a canon of forty-five Āgamas (11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 10 Prakīrṇakas, 6 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras, 2 Cūlikāsūtras) together with the niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi and ṭīkā layers
Worship of consecrated images of the Jinas (Jina-pūjā) in temples as a support for the inner state; material worship (dravya-pūjā) is for householders, inner worship (bhāva-pūjā) for all
Pilgrimage to the tīrthas (Śatruñjaya, Girnār, Ābu, Sammeda Śikhara) and consecration rites re-enacting the five kalyāṇakas
Organized in gacchas (Tapā, Kharatara, Añcala and others) that differ in ritual details and calendars
summary: The image-worshipping majority of the Śvetāmbaras, who accept forty-five Āgamas with their commentaries, worship Jina images in temples and are organized in monastic lineages called gacchas; the Tapā Gaccha is today the largest.

name: Sthānakavāsī

tradition.text: Loṅkā Śāh's reform in the 15th c. (c. 1451/1476 CE); the Sthānakavāsī orders formed by Lavjī, Dharmasiṃha and Dharmadāsa in the 17th c.

distinctive_positions: Rejects the worship of images: the thirty-two Āgamas it accepts contain no injunction to image worship, and worship with water, flowers and fire harms living beings
Accepts thirty-two Āgamas: 11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 4 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras and the Āvaśyaka; rejects the Prakīrṇakas and later commentarial layers as authorities
Monks and nuns wear the mouth-cloth (mukhavastrikā) at all times to protect beings of the air
Religious life centres on the 'sthānaka' (hall for monks and for lay sāmāyika), not the temple
summary: The non-image-worshipping Śvetāmbara order descending from the 15th-century critic Loṅkā Śāh and the 17th-century reformers Lavjī, Dharmasiṃha and Dharmadāsa. It accepts thirty-two Āgamas, rejects temple worship, and its mendicants always wear the mouth-cloth; many groups united in the Śramaṇa Saṅgha in 1952.

name: Śvetāmbara Terāpanth
alt_names: Terāpantha ('the path of thirteen' / 'your path, Lord')

tradition.text: founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu on leaving the Sthānakavāsī ācārya Raghunāth in 1760 CE (Vikrama 1817)

distinctive_positions: One ācārya governs the whole order; all monks and nuns are initiated by and answerable to him, under a written code (maryādā)
Accepts thirty-two Āgamas and rejects image worship

Distinguishes worldly (laukika) duty from spiritual (lokottara) dharma: only acts that stop karmic inflow and foster self-restraint are dharma; saving or feeding the unrestrained is not in itself spiritual merit (a disputed position)
In the 20th c. (recent): the Aṇuvrata movement (Tulsī), the samaṇ/samaṇī intermediate order and prekṣā-dhyāna (Mahāprajña)
summary: A strictly centralized Śvetāmbara order founded in 1760 by Ācārya Bhikṣu, who broke with the Sthānakavāsīs over laxity and over what counts as dharma. It is aniconic, has a single ācārya, and is known in recent times for Ācārya Tulsī's Aṇuvrata movement and Ācārya Mahāprajña's prekṣā meditation.

name: Digambara

tradition.text: the Digambaras regard themselves as continuing the original naked practice of Mahāvīra; their account traces the division to Bhadrabāhu's migration south during a twelve-year famine (Maurya period)

scholarly.text: a distinct Digambara identity is attested from roughly the early centuries CE; the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kundakunda's works are dated by scholars between the 2nd and 8th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Complete nudity is required of the fully renounced monk; one who wears clothes cannot attain liberation
Liberation is not possible in a female body; a woman must first be reborn as a man (nuns, āryikās, keep a white robe and are ranked with the most advanced laity)
The omniscient does not take food (no kavalāhāra); hunger and thirst are among the eighteen faults absent in the Jina
The original Aṅgas and Pūrvas were gradually lost; only portions survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa; the Śvetāmbara Āgamas are not accepted
Scripture is arranged in four anuyogas (narrative, cosmological-karmic, conduct, substance)
In Mahāvīra's life: no embryo transfer, sixteen dreams of the mother, and no marriage; Mallinātha was a man
summary: The 'sky-clad' branch of the Jain tradition, whose monks go naked and eat once a day from their hands. It holds that the Aṅgas were lost and bases itself on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa and the works of Kundakunda, Umāsvāti and later ācāryas; it denies liberation in a female body and eating by the omniscient. It includes the Bīsapantha and Terāpantha modes of worship and the aniconic Tāraṇapantha.

name: Yāpanīya
alt_names: Gopya / Āpulīya Saṅgha (names in some sources; low confidence)

tradition.text: Devasena's Darśanasāra (Digambara) says the Yāpanīya saṅgha was founded by Śrīkalaśa at Kalyāṇa (date given in the Vikrama era; low confidence)

scholarly.text: attested in Karnataka inscriptions from about the 5th c. CE (Kadamba grants) to about the 14th–15th c. CE, after which it disappears

distinctive_positions: Monks went naked and carried the peacock-feather whisk like the Digambaras
Yet held, with the Śvetāmbaras, that women can attain liberation (strī-nirvāṇa) and that the omniscient takes food (kevali-bhukti)
Accepted a form of the old canon (Āvaśyaka, Chedasūtras, niryuktis and others, as cited in Aparājita's commentary) rather than declaring it lost
Allowed that those who wear clothes by exception (apavāda-liṅga) and householders can in principle be liberated (reported in later sources; moderate confidence)
summary: An extinct Jain order of the Deccan and Karnataka that combined Digambara-style monastic nudity with Śvetāmbara positions on women's liberation and the kevalin's eating. Its chief surviving works are Śākaṭāyana (Pālyakīrti)'s Strīnirvāṇa- and Kevalibhukti-prakaraṇas; Aparājita's commentary on the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā is usually assigned to it.

name: Tapā Gaccha

tradition.text: the name 'Tapā' given in 1228 CE to Jagaccandrasūri for his austerities (tapas) by the ruler of Mewar

distinctive_positions: the largest Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka gaccha; celebrates Saṃvatsarī on the fourth of Bhādrapada (bright half)
reformist in origin, stressing austerity and strict monastic discipline
summary: The largest Mūrtipūjaka monastic lineage, named after Jagaccandrasūri's austerities; its monks include the Mughal-era Hīravijayasūri and the philosopher Yaśovijaya.

name: Kharatara Gaccha

tradition.text: the epithet 'kharatara' ('sharper, keener') given to Jineśvarasūri after his victory over the temple-dwelling monks at Aṇahilapāṭaka in 1024 CE

distinctive_positions: born of the reform against temple-dwelling (caityavāsa) monks, insisting that monks live in lodgings (vasati) given by laypeople
veneration of the four 'Dādāgurus' (Jinadatta, Maṇidhārī Jinacandra, Jinakuśala, Jinacandra) at shrines called dādābāḍīs
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha tracing itself to Jineśvarasūri's 1024 debate against the temple-dwelling monks at the Caulukya court; known for its Dādāguru cult and strong presence in Rajasthan.

name: Añcala Gaccha (Vidhipakṣa)

scholarly.text: 12th c. CE (c. 1156 CE is often given; low confidence)

distinctive_positions: uses the hem (añcala) of the garment instead of the mouth-cloth when laymen perform rites (hence the name, per the usual explanation)
'Vidhipakṣa' — the party of the correct rite; strongest in Kacch
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha founded in the 12th c. by Āryarakṣitasūri as a ritual reform, concentrated in Kacch and among Kacchī Jains.

name: Pārśvacandra Gaccha
distinctive_positions: an early-16th-century offshoot of the Tapā Gaccha; small
summary: A small Mūrtipūjaka gaccha named after Pārśvacandrasūri (16th c.), a Gujarati author of vernacular commentaries (ṭabos) on the Āgamas.

name: Tristuti Gaccha

scholarly.text: revived in the 19th c. by Rājendrasūri (1827–1906)

distinctive_positions: recites only three praise-verses (stuti) in caityavandana, omitting the fourth addressed to the attendant deities (śruta- and śāsana-devatās)
summary: A Mūrtipūjaka gaccha revived by Rājendrasūri, compiler of the Prakrit encyclopaedia Abhidhāna Rājendra, which rejects worship of the guardian deities in the monastic rite.

name: Upakeśa Gaccha
distinctive_positions: claims descent from Pārśva's disciple-line through Keśin, i.e. from before Mahāvīra (the tradition's account)
associated with Osiyā (Upakeśapura) in Marwar and the Osvāl caste
summary: A historical Śvetāmbara gaccha of Marwar that traced itself to Pārśva's lineage via Keśin and is linked to the conversion of the Osvāls at Osiyā; its present status is uncertain.

name: Caityavāsī (temple-dwelling monks)

scholarly.text: prominent c. 5th–11th c. CE in western India; opposed by Haribhadra and defeated in debate by Jineśvarasūri (1024)

distinctive_positions: monks resided permanently in temples, administered their property and handled money — criticized by reformers as contrary to the Āgamas
summary: The temple-dwelling Śvetāmbara monks of early medieval western India, against whom Haribhadra's Sambodhaprakaraṇa and the Kharatara reform (vasativāsa) were directed; their clothed resident successors are sometimes seen in the later yatis and śrīpūjyas.

name: Loṅkā Gaccha
distinctive_positions: rejection of image worship and of monastic laxity on the basis of the Āgamas as copied and read by Loṅkā Śāh
summary: The aniconic Śvetāmbara movement that arose from the teaching of Loṅkā Śāh of Ahmedabad; its later lax 'yatis' were in turn reformed by the founders of the Sthānakavāsī orders.

name: Śramaṇa Saṅgha (Vardhamāna Sthānakavāsī Jain Śramaṇa Saṅgha)

scholarly.text: formed 1952 at the Sādaḍī convention by uniting many Sthānakavāsī sampradāyas

distinctive_positions: a single federated order of formerly separate Sthānakavāsī groups under one ācārya (first: Ātmārām)
summary: The union of most Sthānakavāsī lineages formed in 1952 (recent); several groups remained outside it.

name: Mūla Saṅgha (Digambara)
alt_names: with the Nandi, Sena, Deva and Siṃha gaṇas
distinctive_positions: the 'root' Digambara lineage, claiming descent through Kundakunda (Kundakundānvaya); its bhaṭṭāraka seats and monks use the peacock-feather whisk
summary: The principal historical Digambara monastic lineage, subdivided into gaṇas and gacchas, whose inscriptions name Kundakunda as ancestor; most present Digambara monks and bhaṭṭārakas belong to it.

name: Kāṣṭhā Saṅgha

tradition.text: founded (per Devasena's Darśanasāra) by Kumārasena; dated there in the Vikrama era (low confidence)

distinctive_positions: uses a whisk of yak-tail hair (gopuccha) instead of peacock feathers; accused in the Darśanasāra of permitting women's initiation and other deviations (low confidence)
summary: A Digambara lineage of north and west India (named after the town Kāṣṭhā) condemned as 'false' by Devasena but later accepted as a Digambara branch with its own bhaṭṭārakas.

name: Drāviḍa Saṅgha

tradition.text: founded by Vajranandi, a pupil of Pūjyapāda, at Madhurā (Madurai) according to the Darśanasāra

scholarly.text: c. 5th–13th c. CE in Tamil country and Karnataka

distinctive_positions: charged by the Darśanasāra with allowing monks to eat seeds and to engage in trade and agriculture for temples (low confidence)
summary: A southern Digambara lineage associated with Vajranandi and the Tamil country, criticized in the Darśanasāra; later inscriptions treat it as a respected Digambara saṅgha.

name: Māthura Saṅgha
distinctive_positions: 'niḥpicchika' — its monks carried no whisk at all (per the Darśanasāra; low confidence)
summary: A Digambara lineage named in Devasena's Darśanasāra as founded by Rāmasena; known mainly from Digambara polemic and a few inscriptions.

name: Bīsapantha (Digambara)
distinctive_positions: worship of Jina images with fresh flowers, fruits and lamps and seated worship
acceptance of the bhaṭṭārakas as religious authorities
worship of guardian and attendant deities (Padmāvatī, Kṣetrapāla)
summary: The 'older' mode of Digambara temple practice, loyal to the bhaṭṭāraka institution and to the attendant deities, as distinguished from the reforming Terāpantha.

name: Terāpantha (Digambara)

scholarly.text: 17th c. CE (Agra, Sanganer and Jaipur region), growing out of Banārsīdās's Adhyātma circle

distinctive_positions: rejects the authority of the bhaṭṭārakas
offers only dry and non-living substances (e.g. rice, dry fruits) in image worship, no fresh flowers or lamps, and standing worship
rejects the worship of attendant deities (śāsanadevatās) as wrong faith
summary: A lay-led Digambara reform movement of the 17th–18th c. (not connected with the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth) that rejected the bhaṭṭārakas and reduced image worship to non-harming offerings; Paṇḍit Ṭoḍarmal's Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka is its classic.

name: Tāraṇapantha (Samaiyā)
distinctive_positions: no image worship: its shrines (caityālayas) house scriptures, which are venerated
open to members of all castes; emphasis on the soul's inner nature in Tāraṇa Svāmī's fourteen works
summary: An aniconic Digambara-derived community of central India founded by Tāraṇa Svāmī, whose shrines keep books instead of images.

name: Tamil Jain tradition
regions: Tamil Nadu (Maturai hills, Kāñcīpuram and Tiruparuttikkuṉṟam, Ciṅkavaram, Mēlcittāmūr, Tirumalai)

tradition.text: Tamil Jains trace their teachers to Bhadrabāhu's migration and to Kundakunda (Elācārya); inscriptions in Tamil-Brāhmī in hill caves are claimed as the earliest Jain presence

scholarly.text: Tamil-Brāhmī cave inscriptions c. 2nd c. BCE onward; the Jain literary flowering c. 5th–13th c. CE; decline after the Śaiva revival (7th c. onward)

distinctive_positions: Digambara in doctrine and practice; the monastic seats (maṭhas) at Mēlcittāmūr and Arahantagiri (Tirumalai) with their bhaṭṭārakas
a major literary contribution to Tamil: the Nālaṭiyār and other didactic works, the epics Cīvakacintāmaṇi and Nīlakēci, grammar (Naṉṉūl) and prosody (Yāpparuṅkalam)
summary: The Digambara Jain community of the Tamil country, whose monks and poets produced much of classical Tamil didactic and narrative literature and whose memory of conflict with the Śaiva Nāyaṉmārs is recorded on both sides.
